title: Does China Have Enough Water For Its Thirsty AI Data Centers?
desc:
Does China Have Enough Water For Its Thirsty AI Data Centers?

Authored by James Gorrie via The Epoch Times,

According to China's Ministry of Water Resources, China has nearly one-fifth of the world's population but only about 6 percent of global freshwater resources.

That presents planners in Beijing with a challenging problem: How to support 20 percent of humanity, more than 18 percent of global economic output, and an expanding digital economy, with a disproportionately small water resource?

Things become even more complicated because China's most economically developed regions are not necessarily where water is most abundant.

Now, Beijing wants to build substantially more artificial intelligence (AI) computing capacity. That raises another fundamental question: Can China expand its AI infrastructure without worsening its existing water crisis?

China Is Betting Big on AI Infrastructure

Over the next five years, China is preparing to expand its nationwide AI data center infrastructure by roughly 2 trillion yuan, or $295 billion. The plan would create interconnected computing hubs and rely heavily on domestic technology suppliers.

Rystad Energy estimates China's installed data-center capacity reached about 32 gigawatts at the end of 2025 and could rise above 60 gigawatts by 2030. Data-center electricity consumption could reach 289 terawatt-hours by 2030, more than twice 2025 levels. AI and high-performance computing are expected to drive much of that growth.

But electricity is only half the infrastructure equation. Since AI servers generate enormous amounts of heat, data centers must rely on cooling technologies that require substantial amounts of water.

What's more, China's existing data centers are already using a lot of it.

China's Data Centers Already Have a Water Problem

A 2025 study published in Applied Energy provides perhaps the clearest warning.

Researchers estimated that China's data centers consumed approximately 15.7 billion cubic meters of water in 2022, equivalent to about 2.7 percent of China's total water consumption. Even more significant, the researchers found that 72 percent of China's computing capacity was located in regions experiencing severe water scarcity.

The Chinese regime has been trying to move computing capacity away from the crowded eastern regions toward western provinces where electricity, particularly renewable electricity, is more readily available.

The strategy makes sense from an energy perspective, but not so much from a water supply perspective. The same study found that China's "Eastern Data and Western Computing" strategy could increase water-footprint pressures in water-scarce western regions such as Gansu and Ningxia.

The imbalance between China's water supply and rising cooling needs is obvious. Beijing is solving one bottleneck while creating another.

Moving Data West Doesn't Move the Water

This is the central problem with China's strategy. Western provinces have vast solar and wind resources and enormous areas available for data-center construction. But parts of the west are also among China's driest regions.

That creates a fundamental trade-off because China cannot simply allocate more water to AI without hurting other key areas. Water used to cool an AI data center competes, directly or indirectly, with agricultural, industrial, municipal, and ecological needs.

Agriculture accounted for about 62 percent of China's total water use in 2025, compared with 16 percent for industry and 15.8 percent for domestic consumption. Total national water use reached approximately 594.45 billion cubic meters. Agriculture's dominance matters because food security is a strategic priority for Beijing.

On the flip side, China is improving efficiency. Water consumption per 10,000 yuan of GDP fell 4.5 percent in 2025, while water consumption per 10,000 yuan of industrial value-added declined 7.2 percent.

Those gains are significant, but efficiency cannot eliminate scarcity.

If AI computing grows rapidly enough, a data center can become more water-efficient even as the overall sector consumes more water.

That's the danger.

China Is Trying to Make AI Greener

Beijing has set a goal to source 80 percent of its data-center electricity from green energy by 2030, up from 11 percent in 2023. But analysts say AI's highly variable computing loads make it difficult to integrate data centers smoothly with renewable power systems.

The regime is also encouraging higher efficiency in data centers by improving power and water usage effectiveness. That technology can make a major difference.

The Applied Energy study found that simultaneous improvements in power efficiency, water efficiency, and electricity-grid decarbonization could reduce China's national data-center water footprint by 51.5 percent to 58.3 percent by 2050, compared with a business-as-usual scenario.

The bad news is that these are scenarios, not guarantees.

The AI Boom Could Outrun the Efficiency Gains

China's data-center industry is expanding as AI demand grows. The same technological advances that make AI more useful also increase demand for computing power.

Rystad Energy expects Chinese data-center electricity consumption to grow at roughly 19 percent annually between 2025 and 2030. But those efficiency improvements may not offset the water consequences of rapidly increasing computational capacity.

The result could be a familiar economic pattern of more efficient machines on the one hand, but more of those machines on the other.

This is where China's water dilemma becomes more serious. It can reduce the amount of water required per unit of computing while still increasing total water consumption.

What Happens If Water Becomes the Bottleneck?

If water becomes scarce around major AI hubs, China could face pressure to restrict where new data centers are built. That could increase infrastructure costs and force companies to move computing capacity toward regions with better water availability.

It could also increase competition among agriculture, cities, and manufacturing and technology companies. That matters because China's economy is already heavily dependent on water-intensive industries and food production.

China can build reservoirs, pipelines, water-transfer systems, recycling facilities, and increasingly efficient industrial infrastructure. It can force industries to meet state-directed efficiency targets. But it can't manufacture freshwater at the scale necessary to meet the underlying demands of AI, industry, agriculture, and public use.

Water is ultimately constrained by geography and climate and could become one of the least visible but most important constraints on China's AI expansion through the 2030s.

Views expressed in this article are opinions of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of The Epoch Times or ZeroHedge.

title: "It's A Pity...": Zelensky Feels 'Betrayed' By Trump & Elon Musk
desc:
"It's A Pity...": Zelensky Feels 'Betrayed' By Trump & Elon Musk

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says he feels betrayed by President Trump in the wake of the US deal to buy Russian fuel from Moscow, which was announced last week.

Zelensky went on a newly aired episode of Piers Morgan's show, and he was asked point blank by the British show host if he had been "betrayed" by the Trump administration, to which Zelensky answered, "Really, Yes." Russian media was quick to seize on the increasingly open schism between Trump and Zelensky...

Zelensky tells Piers Morgan he feels 'BETRAYED' BY TRUMP: 'really YES, really, between us' https://t.co/InYEjF5LLa

— RT (@RT_com) October 14, 2026

"It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner," the Ukrainian leader told Morgan on Wednesday.

"This is our country, our body, our home, our children… That's why it’s painful when Trump chooses one side," Zelensky at one point also stated.

"If you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle. Not on the wrong side," said Zelensky. "This is not the right side of history." Here, Zelensky seemed to suggest Trump is actually more on the Kremlin side of things at this point.

The interview also came amid reports that the US is throttling intelligence-sharing with Kiev. The White House has thus far neither confirmed nor denied the allegations.

Zelensky on Trump: If you're in the middle, you have to stay in the middle, not on the wrong side. I think Trump's advisers are wrong. I don't know who is pushing him to the wrong side. This is not the right side of history. https://t.co/RyMNITUUFY

— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 14, 2026

But Zelensky has himself for the past two night of Russian airstrikes made a point to publicize that Western partners have not provided the typical early warning notices of inbound missiles that were available in prior such attacks.

There's been another apparently 'betrayal' (in Zelensky's assessment) by the White House of late: reports say that SpaceX has imposed a movement-speed restriction on certain Starlink terminals used in Ukraine.

This has deeply impacted Ukraine's military, which is greatly reliant on Starlink for rapid battlefield communications and functions. Zelensky used the Piers Morgan appears to plead that it be 'switched on'.

Ukraine is not a partner of the United States. Ukraine is a toy they've grown tired of playing with. ---- Zelensky to Elon Musk: On Starlink, we are asking to switch it on. https://t.co/jW1zEg60qC

— Marta Havryshko (@HavryshkoMarta) October 14, 2026

"People will die, of course, if attacks will continue and if Starlink will not work… it’s not helpful," he continued.

The Ukrainian leader expressed home the limitation was merely a "mistake," suggesting it could "maybe a huge technical problem" at SpaceX.

Overall, Zelensky's message was that Ukraine is 'losing' American support and that he feels betrayed not only be Trump, but by Elon Musk too.

Musk has directly chimed in on the controversy, clarifying "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government" - and so ultimately it's the US government, not SpaceX, behind whatever cut happened that impacted Ukraine.

Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.

title: People Who Bought MAGA Hats!? Jack Smith's Arctic Frost Hoovered Up Data On At Least 639,000 Republican Voters, Donors
desc:
People Who Bought MAGA Hats!? Jack Smith's Arctic Frost Hoovered Up Data On At Least 639,000 Republican Voters, Donors

Former special counsel Jack Smith's office and the Biden Justice Department obtained spreadsheets on "over 639,000 individuals, at minimum" - Republican donors, supporters and voters - according to a new memo from Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, first reported by Fox News Digital on Wednesday. Grassley's account rests on whistleblower disclosures to his committee.

Of those, more than 148,000 rows are identified in the spreadsheets as donors, who generally gave small amounts. The data includes names, dates of birth, home addresses, emails, whether the person is a registered Republican, occupation and employer, credit card information, donor analysis data and donation amounts. Grassley said samples on the list included retirees, pool technicians, drivers and loggers.

The Daily Caller reports that the trove also covers the shipping addresses of people who bought MAGA hats, and that it reaches back to 2005. The Fox account of the memo does not mention hat buyers, so that detail rests on the Daily Caller's reading.

"This update shows that Jack Smith and the Biden Justice Department collected incredibly invasive donor data - and voter data - beyond what could conceivably be necessary" for the special counsel's mandate, Grassley said. He added that it "corroborates that Smith and his partisan team aimed to map out the entire Republican Party apparatus," and again called on Senate Judiciary Democrats to join his oversight work.

Smith told the committee on Sept. 29 that his team "acquired financial information." Pressed by Grassley for a yes or no on whether his office obtained donor data, Smith answered "Yes," according to Fox's account, and said he could not "recite to you every subpoena we issued." He said the subpoenas served a criminal investigation and that he had "a duty to collect facts." Smith's newly launched law firm did not immediately respond to Fox's request for comment, and no response from Smith or the Justice Department to the new memo had appeared in the coverage reviewed.

The memo follows an earlier Grassley release, also drawn from whistleblower records. On the day of the hearing, the committee's Republicans said Smith's team acquired at least 4,782 checks from donors to President Trump and Trump-aligned Republican entities, written between September 2019 and August 2023 in all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico. The checks show home addresses, bank account and routing numbers and signatures, and were routed to former FBI Special Agent Walter Giardina, the release says. Grassley said some gave as little as $1, that 42 of the checks came from Iowans, and that "the Justice Department and FBI will forever possess thousands of people's addresses."

At the hearing, Smith defended secretly obtaining Republican lawmakers' phone records. He could not say whether his subpoenas sought the lawmakers' physical locations, and could not recall key details about his demands for conservative fundraising information, the Washington Examiner reported.

The donor material fits a pattern Grassley has been releasing for a year. In October 2025 he made public 197 subpoenas sent to 34 individuals and 163 businesses, seeking records tied to at least 430 named Republican individuals and entities, including statistical data and analysis on donors and fundraising. "This was clearly a fishing expedition," he said then. In July, Grassley said records showed Smith's team obtained and reviewed texts involving 44 current and former lawmakers, and House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan said Congress was weighing a criminal referral over Smith's testimony about those records.

Smith is now fighting on several fronts. As we reported earlier this month, Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., sued him over the seizure of lawmakers' phone records, seeking $1 in damages, and Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., filed a bar complaint recommending disbarment.

title: Asia Scrambles For Coal As Energy Crisis Sends Prices To Two-Year High Ahead Of Winter
desc:
Asia Scrambles For Coal As Energy Crisis Sends Prices To Two-Year High Ahead Of Winter

As the Northern Hemisphere winter quickly approaches, Asian thermal coal prices have climbed to two-year highs and could be on the cusp of a major breakout as utilities stockpile the dirty fuel amid disruptions to natural gas and crude product markets caused by the war in Ukraine and the Strait of Hormuz disruption.

Newcastle coal futures, an Asian benchmark, are up more than 40% on the year and could surge even higher if the $150-a-ton level is sustained.

Prices on Tuesday closed at their highest levels since August 2024.

The combination of Ukraine decimating Russian refineries with drone attacks and the Strait of Hormuz disruptions to energy flows has sparked a global refining crisis that has encouraged utilities to switch from higher-priced natural gas and heating oil to cheaper alternative fuels such as coal.

Morgan Stanley analysts led by Amy Gower wrote in a note last week that the global refining crisis has made "the long-term outlook for thermal coal demand more resilient." They raised their long-term outlook for Newcastle export prices by 4% to $125 a ton.

According to Bloomberg, China's coal output has fallen more than 3% in the first eight months of the year after a deadly mining accident earlier this year triggered safety inspections and prolonged shutdowns.

Wood Mackenzie analyst Hangyu Li expects more Chinese mines to get the green light to restart, but any new production would come as a lag.

"We expect more mines to gradually win approval to restart after about four months of suspension, but a quick rebound on production in the near-term is unlikely," Li wrote in the note.

Possible relief from a harsh winter could come from above-normal temperatures forecast across Asia because of a record-breaking El Niño, which would ease heating demand.

title: Mohammed bin Salman Is More At Risk Internally Than From Houthi Attacks
desc:
Mohammed bin Salman Is More At Risk Internally Than From Houthi Attacks

Authored by Alastair Crooke

As part of its “blockade-for-blockade,” “airport-for-airport” strategy, Ansarallah carried out a third attack on Riyadh International Airport on Saturday — 12 people (mostly civilians) were killed and more than 300 injured. This, in tandem with Iran’s escalating attacks on tankers, and expanding its maritime operations, immediately increases the pressures on President Trump to respond — at the precise moment when midterm elections loom.

As the military conflict between Yemen and Saudi Arabia continues, the latter has become increasingly dependent on attacks against Yemeni civilian targets — by Sept 2025, reports confirm that “nearly 15,000 civilians have been killed by direct military action, most of them in air strikes by the Saudi-led Coalition.” Yet the Yemeni armed resistance, taking its cue from Iran’s experience, sees that Saudi is infinitely more vulnerable via its energy infrastructure sitting out in the open.

If Yemen continues to strike at key Saudi economic and energy assets with precision, the consequences for Riyadh will multiply — the battlefield will increasingly become that of Saudi infrastructure destruction and pain for the West versus Yemeni civilian casualties.

This scenario could lead to major capital destruction, a sovereign debt crisis, and Riyadh forced to abandon yet more of its Vision 2030 projects on which MbS has staked the kingdom’s future.

Saudi Arabia continues to behave as though the old formulas of sectarianism, anti-Iran propaganda and an anti-Shia narrative can once again be used to maintain their pro-Western positioning. But those tired mantra have lost their effectiveness — even among large parts of the region’s Sunnis.

The situation today is fundamentally different. AnsarAllah does not represent the Twelver Shia framework that Saudi propaganda could easily portray as an “Iranian project.” AnsarAllah-governed Yemen has its own ideological framework, theological traditions, political history, and system of governance. Neither AnsarAllah nor the broader pro-Sana’a camp can simply be reduced to one sect or social class.

The AnsarAllah Yemeni landscape includes Hanafi Sunnis, Zaidis, Jaroodiya, Ismailis, and other Islamic schools, with even elements of Salafi groups existing within the broader Yemeni social structure.

In short, unless MbS capitulates to AnsarAllah demands — which it seems he is incapable of so doing — the consequences could develop into a devastating macro-economic cascade occurring within the key pivot situated at the center of the Gulf economic model; a cascade, furthermore, which, as its momentum grows, and foreign capital flees the kingdom, will bring a systemic collapse to the entire western colonial enterprise in the Gulf.

The more paradoxical element to this drama is that it is not from AnsarAllah’s attacks that MbS’ is most at risk — or from which his downfall might be precipitated. It will not come from the battlefield either. Regime change inside Saudi Arabia will come about as a result of his own hand — his compulsive quest to centralize control.

Even Edward Luttwak, known for his links to the western security state, observes that —

…the reason for [the impotence] of Saudi Arabia, in the face of the Houthi offensive, is that, for the Kingdom’s ruling family, the most deadly danger has long been a military coup d’état — such as the one which ended Iraq’s monarchy and killed every single member of its Husseini ruling family on 14 July 1958.

Against that danger, the successive heads of the Saudi ruling family have implemented the most effective remedy possible: divide and rule, not against foreign enemies, but within their own armed forces. For that reason, the different combat elements of the armed forces are geographically separated in the country’s vast territory, and commanded by different princes in charge of various parts of the ministry of defence, all of which are subordinate to the minister himself, Prince Khalid (a younger brother of Mohammed bin Salman).

MbS’ fear is that one F15 pilot, outside of the privileged Royal family Stipendiary circle, might choose to attack one of the Kingdom’s princely palaces (instead of striking at an AnsarAllah target) as a prelude to an all-out military revolt. This is no fanciful threat — an old “Saudi hand” recalled recently hearing one young Saudi officer threatening to do exactly that.

By cutting off traditional tribal patronage by which tribal leaders had expected to receive their share of the kingdom’s oil wealth; by seizing tribal lands earmarked for MbS “vanity projects”; and by actively working to reshape Saudi Arabia’s core legitimacy away from traditional tribal-religious alliances towards a nationalist, youth-driven identity centred around Vision 2030, MbS has cut away the political leverage that traditional tribal elders historically held within the Royal Court.

MBS has made many enemies through the transformation of the Kingdom not towards a nation-state, but rather toward being the property of a single family. He has concentrated immense political, economic, and security powers within his immediate branch of the family, acting as an absolute authority.

As one commentator writes —

For traditional tribal groups like the ‘Anizah, this means that policy decisions are made strictly from the top down, leaving little room for the traditional consensus-building or special autonomy that tribes historically enjoyed.

The erosion of the historic social contract has left a deep sense of economic anxiety and loss of prestige among traditional tribal structures — and among the Wahhabi religious establishment.

The result is that —

…a tribal realignment is under way. In the north and central areas, the Shammar and Anizzah desert tribes have reportedly sealed the borders to Jordan and Iraq. In the south, mountain tribes with historical kinship ties to AnsarAllah are more likely to ignore the border with Yemen than defend the crown.

And we’ll know, soon enough, whether there is any foundation to the [multiple] rumors that representatives of more than a dozen Saudi tribes have sat with IRGC representatives and floated a new political compact — a federal state with tribes receiving a share of oil and gas revenues.

It wouldn’t be surprising if there are not other tribes and clans throughout the Region (Syria, Iraq …) who have a similar smoldering resentment to that of the Saudi tribes, festering secretly away, and similarly derived from their own experience of top-down colonial exploitation.

Might the Saudi Kingdom experience a revolt against MbS? Such a possibility is not without precedent: When King Saud’s reckless governance threatened the monarchy’s survival in 1964, the family, senior princes, and the religious leadership stepped in to strip him of power and enforce his abdication.

In the event of the collapse of MbS-led al-Saud family rule, this would not only topple the Gulf colonial project, but would then initiate a scramble for a fundamental geopolitical re-alignment of the region.

The colonial “current shape” imposed upon West Asia for more than a century is at an inflection point. Everything is “up in the air.” How will President Trump react to AnsarAllah’s accelerated attacks on Saudi Arabia? Will he launch a wider war across the region by attacking Iran, Yemen or Iraq? Or will a major attack on north Yemen against Ansarallah, with Pakistani and Israeli participation, be authorised? Or might the Sistan-Baluchistan region of Iran erupt as a result of a Pakistani-CIA insertion of cross-border Balochi insurgents into Iran, potentially leading to Iranian exchanges of fire with Pakistan?

We don’t know. But it is widely understood that the region’s current shape was drawn up for other, earlier purposes — Bahrain was Persian for two centuries before 1783; Kuwait was a district of Basra until Britain drew a line of separation in 1899; the United Arab Emirates were Trucial Oman (coastal sheikhdoms under British protection, until December 1971). Qatar was a Bahraini suzerainty, then Ottoman, then British, before it became a state in 1971. Lebanon and Syria were carved out of the Ottoman ruin by France in 1920. Jordan was proclaimed a “state” by a British High Commissioner in 1921.

Luttwak forewarns that — “Ultimately… the [al-Saud] inheritors must learn to share Saudi Arabia’s vast flow of oil revenues with everybody else, or else risk losing more than just their wealth.”

Iran has just launched large-scale military exercises amid indications of a possible imminent Israeli-American escalation to come very soon.

Change seems inevitable.

title: Trump Doubles Down On $5,000 Payments Tied To Midterm Results
desc:
Trump Doubles Down On $5,000 Payments Tied To Midterm Results

President Trump released a new video ad this week repeating his pledge of $5,000 for every adult citizen if Republicans keep the House and the Senate in the Nov. 4 midterms.

"I'm going to give all adult citizens in the United States of America $5,000," Trump said in the video, posted to X.

"Democrat policies won't allow this to happen. In fact, the opposite."

TRUMP POSTS A VIDEO SAYING HE'LL GIVE EVERY ADULT U.S. CITIZEN $5,000 IF REPUBLICANS WIN THE MIDTERMS pic.twitter.com/tYYPnY4yew

— A y l a (@Callme_ayla00) October 14, 2026

If the GOP wins Congress, "you will each have $5,000 in your pocket, and economic success for our country like we have never ever seen before," he said, adding that Democrats would raise taxes or even create "an economic depression."

He made the same promise at an Oct. 7 rally in San Antonio for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Local12 reported, without saying how it would be funded or whether Congress would have to approve it. At roughly 270 million adult citizens, $5,000 each would cost about $1.35 trillion, by ZeroHedge's math on the headcount.

As the Epoch Times notes further, the president first made reference to the payments last month during a speech in Dallas designed to boost Republican voter turnout during the midterms, although some members of his own party have publicly said they do not support the plan.

In one example of GOP pushback, Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) wrote in a post on X about the dividend payment proposal: "Some of us think dependency is evil [and] soul-sucking in all its forms."

Among Democrats, many have said that the proposal would add to the U.S. national debt and increase inflation.

In a post to X several weeks ago, Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) accused the president of trying "to pay off voters" in a bid that he said "would explode the deficit, drive up the cost of home and auto loans, and send inflation skyrocketing."

The White House would likely need congressional approval to send out the payments, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said in a Sept. 13 CNN interview. But Trump said at about the same time, in a CBS interview, that he may not need lawmakers to act.

Since last month's Dallas event, Trump has frequently made reference to the possible payments in speeches and on social media, including during a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, over the past weekend.

"If Republicans win the House of Representatives and the Senate ... I am going to give all adult citizens in the United States of America $5,000," Trump said at the event. "Only Republicans can do it."

Tariff revenue would pay for those payments, he said at the Oct. 9 Clarksville event. He also suggested that new factories, plants, and other investments would create revenue and enough economic growth to cover the costs.

In a separate announcement, Trump also said his administration is sending health insurance-related rebate payments to certain people, including those who he said were overcharged via Affordable Care Act exchanges and to seniors enrolled in Medicare Part B.

An email that was seen by The Epoch Times last week, sent by Trump, indicated that $90 payments to Medicare recipients were going out. Some 20 million people would get the payments, the email states.

Last month, Trump released a social media video announcing that $500 rebate payments would be sent to nearly 1 million people who the administration stated were overcharged via Obamacare health care exchanges under the Biden administration.

title: No Quick Pump Relief: IEA Warns Diesel Squeeze Will Persist Into 2027
desc:
No Quick Pump Relief: IEA Warns Diesel Squeeze Will Persist Into 2027

Goldman energy analyst Nikhil Bhandari warned last month that a deepening refining crisis could prolong diesel and gasoline pain at the pump well into 2027. Now, the International Energy Agency is reinforcing that warning, cautioning that diesel supplies could remain tight into the second half of next year.

"The gasoil market balance will remain tight well into 2027 and is dependent on a recovery of product supply from the Middle East. Failing this, further demand reductions and the heavy economic costs these will entail may be needed to balance markets," the IEA wrote in its Oil Market Report for October.

The report continued, "Global gasoil markets tightened counter-seasonally in 3Q26, as prolonged disruptions to Middle Eastern and Russian exports forced stock draws. Combined with much heavier-than-normal inventory declines in 2Q26, this has deprived global gasoil markets of crucial stock cover ahead of the peak winter demand season."

In response, governments are slashing fuel taxes, subsidizing consumers, and draining strategic reserves as diesel prices hit records across the world. Those measures can cushion the immediate shock, but the IEA forecasts that "even with a rapid recovery expected in refinery throughputs into year-end, gasoil supply falls short of meeting demand in 4Q26, suggesting that the replenishment of lost inventories, outside of typical seasonal fluctuations, is unlikely before 2H27."

The combination of Ukraine decimating Russian refineries with drone attacks and ongoing Strait of Hormuz disruptions has pushed the world into a refining crisis. If these pressures continue, they could keep the market from balancing in the first half of next year, sending prices even higher, and unleash a more brutal period of demand destruction. That means businesses and consumers cutting fuel use because prices are too high, with consequences for transport, agriculture, and industrial activity. Higher fuel prices could also feed into inflation, push government bond yields higher, and weigh on global equity markets.

With US diesel prices at the pump topping $6.50 a gallon (data via AAA) last month, the industrial fuel squeeze pushed President Trump last week toward an unlikely source of relief: Russia.

In recent days, Trump said he struck a deal with Moscow to immediately supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the global market, seeking to ease shortages ahead of the US midterm elections.

The Trump administration also pushed the Group of Seven wealthy democracies to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming weeks to cap prices ahead of the Northern Hemisphere winter.

On Tuesday, Vice President JD Vance announced that the administration would use wartime authority to increase fuel production at a refinery in Texas: "I am pleased to announce that the Trump administration, working with the refinery at Delek, has used the Defense Production Act and we're going to expand the refinery right here in Tyler, Texas."

"We want millions of gallons of commercial-grade and military-spec fuel to come out of this refinery, in addition to what it's already producing," Vance told the crowd.

Circling back to Goldman analyst Bhandari's note on the diesel crisis, which could extend well into 2027, he gave clients three scenarios for where global product inventories could head next.

Read the report here. Also read: Goldman commodity experts Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby and Daan Struyven recently warned that the diesel crisis is setting up the next gasoline squeeze.

title: Trump Admin Looking To Strip Ilhan Omar's Citizenship, Then Deport Her; Passport Seized In Raid
desc:
Trump Admin Looking To Strip Ilhan Omar's Citizenship, Then Deport Her; Passport Seized In Raid

The Trump administration wants to strip Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) of her US citizenship and then deport her, according to US officials and others familiar with the case who spoke to the Wall Street Journal.

What's more, DHS agents who searched Omar's Washington home early Monday secured her passport, along with her cellphone, personal computers and notebooks while Omar and her husband stood around watching, the report continues. Over a dozen subpoenas have also gone out for testimony before a Minnesota grand jury, some of them to Omar's relatives, and the family's immigration paperwork is one of the things prosecutors are combing through.

Investigators want to know whether Omar or her father listed her as 17 rather than 18 on her citizenship paperwork, according to the paper's sources. The one-year difference decides how she became a citizen: a child under 18 could pick up citizenship automatically through a parent's naturalization, while an 18-year-old would have needed to go through the process on her own. Omar became a citizen in 2000.

Her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, brought the family to the US in 1995 from a Kenyan refugee camp. He drove a cab and worked for the Postal Service, and died in June 2020 at 67 of Covid-19 complications, according to Omar. The probe is looking at his conduct as well as hers.

Homeland Security Investigations examined a similar tip under Biden and dropped it for lack of evidence of fraud, according to people familiar with that review.

Omar told the Journal earlier this year that she never committed immigration fraud. "President Trump would love to eliminate one of the most effective progressive voices in Congress. There is no basis for this," her office said in a statement Wednesday.

Trump, meanwhile, has called for Omar's deportation for years. On Monday evening, hours after the search, an Ohio crowd he was addressing broke into chants of "deport" after he turned to Omar and Somalis. "They cheat on everything," Trump said, according to the paper.

Watch video

The denaturalization route matters because of the calendar. As we noted on Tuesday, federal prosecutors have ten years to bring criminal charges for naturalization and passport fraud, which puts anything filed in 2000 out of reach. Civil denaturalization cases have no statute of limitations, and relatives who derived citizenship through a parent can lose it too, according to the Congressional Research Service. The Justice Department still has to sue in federal court and prove, by "clear, unequivocal, and convincing" evidence, that citizenship was obtained through a material lie.

The administration has filed more than 200 denaturalization suits this term, which officials tout as the most sweeping such effort in DOJ history. Before Trump's return, the government filed about 12 or fewer annually, according to Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse data cited by the paper. Most of the new cases are still undecided. Omar's, if it is filed, would be the highest-profile yet.

As we reported Monday, HSI agents executed a court-authorized warrant at the house around 6 a.m., and the Justice Department called it part of an ongoing criminal investigation without saying more. The New York Times reported that the warrant cites false statements, immigration-paperwork fraud and conspiracy, according to Newsweek, and that the grand jury has subpoenaed Omar's sister, Sahra Noor. Vice President JD Vance said he had no advance notice of the search, and Trump said it was "really up to the DOJ."

The age question has a paper trail. On Tuesday we flagged emails showing Omar's congressional staff asked Minnesota's Legislative Reference Library in May 2019 to change her listed birth year from 1981 to 1982, days after a viral video questioned her age. The library's legislator page now gives her birth date as Oct. 4, 1982. Under the 1981 date, Omar was 18 for all of 2000; under 1982, she was 17 until that October. The emails don't say what documentation, if any, backed the change.

Separately, Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney in Washington, said Tuesday on Fox News that her office is investigating Omar's financial disclosures, which put her husband Tim Mynett's two businesses at as much as $30 million for 2024 before an April amendment cut the couple's reported assets to $18,004-$95,000. Back in April we noted Omar's sudden discovery that she is not a multimillionaire after all. In September, the Office of Congressional Conduct recommended that the House Ethics Committee dismiss the allegations. Pirro waved that off: "It doesn't matter what the House does," she said.

The immigration allegations have followed Omar since her 2016 run for the Minnesota House, often tied to her marriages. Last month, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a conservative podcast that the investigation was ongoing and claimed Omar "married her brother" to get him into the country - something Trump has frequently claimed as well.

title: Report Alleges Houthis Building Advanced Missiles With Help From China
desc:
Report Alleges Houthis Building Advanced Missiles With Help From China

It should come as no surprise that Iran maintains powerful allies even while under threat of US bombs, and as Washington sanctions have sought its complete isolation. Most obvious among these remain Russia and China - nations which have not necessarily sought to 'hide' or conceal political and even military support to Tehran.

The last several weeks have seen a new Iran conflict-related front opened up in the Middle East. Saudi Arabia and the Ansar Allah movement of Yemen (the Houthis) are now in a state of open war.

Houthi ballistic missiles are raining down on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities on a daily basis, resulting in a full-blown crisis for the kingdom, which is urging allies to come to its defense.

A fresh report in The Wall Street Journal finds that Chinese parts are becoming a key element of some new Houthi missile systems - weapons which have been a surprise and shock to the kingdom and its Western allies, given the number of impacts on targets of late.

"Houthi militants are attempting to produce their own advanced medium-range ballistic missiles using Chinese-delivered parts, a new report shows, a technological advance that would raise the threat posed by the Iran-backed group," WSJ writes.

The report relies heavily on the findings of an international weapons and conflict monitor:

The Houthis shipped in from a Chinese supplier a range of components needed to make a version of one of Iran’s most powerful weapons, the Kheibar Shekan Iranian precision-guided missile, said the report by Conflict Armament Research, a group that works in conflict zones and reports on the use of weapons and their supply chains. The Houthi missile would have a range up to about 1,200 miles, putting all of Saudi Arabia and Israel within reach.

Iran used the Kheibar Shekan—a cheap, mobile, precision weapon first displayed in Tehran in 2022—against American bases with some success during the war with the U.S. last spring, The Wall Street Journal has previously reported.

One caveat here might be to point out that Chinese components in complex electrical or even weapons systems are diffuse across the world - so it remains a big open question how 'direct' or not the supply chain might be in this case.

However, Conflict Armament Research has sought to answer this. "The local ambition of the Houthis for manufacturing is beyond what was previously assumed,” said Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at the organization. "These types of parts are very specific, and producing them would have required design information related to the missile."

As for China's official stance on the ratcheting conflict, its foreign ministry on Monday condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi airports. "China condemns the attacks that caused heavy casualties and expresses serious concern over the intensification of the conflict," foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said.

"We call on relevant parties to avoid taking actions that escalate regional tensions, to resolve differences and disputes through dialogue and negotiation, and to achieve peace and stability in the region at an early date," Mao added. It would be an explosive and highly sensitive situation if Beijing were actually directly assisting a non-state actor like the Houthis in missile development. This is something China will likely vehemently deny.

title: Congresswoman Warns Incoming Socialists Are "National Security Threat," Wants Their Access To Intel Limited
desc:
Congresswoman Warns Incoming Socialists Are "National Security Threat," Wants Their Access To Intel Limited

Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, (R-N.Y.), said two members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) who appear headed to Congress could pose a national security risk, and she wants House leadership to keep them away from sensitive intelligence.

"These people are extreme, they're radical, they are dangerous, and they really have no business being in the United States House of Representatives," Malliotakis, the only Republican representing New York City in the House, told Fox News Digital. "And it scares me that they're going to have access to intelligence."

The two candidates, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Assemblywoman Claire Valdez, won upset primaries this year over establishment-backed opponents in deep-blue districts. Their races made New York City one of the main battlegrounds in this midterm cycle's fight inside the Democratic Party, and both nominees are all but certain to win in November.

Chevalier defeated Rep. Adriano Espaillat, (D-N.Y.), chairman of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, in his district covering Upper Manhattan and parts of the Bronx. Valdez won the open seat spanning parts of Brooklyn and Queens that retiring Rep. Nydia Velazquez, (D-N.Y.), currently holds.

Both candidates have called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and have described Israel's war in Gaza as a "genocide."

Malliotakis said the pair's support for the DSA platform makes them "un-American."

"I think they want to undermine the country. I mean, anybody whose campaign is based on no jails, no cops, no borders, is a real detriment to the country," she said.

The congresswoman directed her concerns at House Speaker Mike Johnson, (R-La.), and urged him to examine whether the incoming members present a security risk.

"These are the people that are going to have access to intelligence? I think [Speaker Mike Johnson] really needs to look at that and see if they're a national security threat," Malliotakis said.

If Republicans hold the House majority in November, Malliotakis wants Johnson to restrict which committees Chevalier and Valdez can join.

"I do have a lot of concern about these members having access to sensitive information and intelligence that if put in the wrong hands, could be a detriment to our national security," she said.

Malliotakis's warning follows reporting earlier this year on the DSA's contacts with Beijing. Newsweek reported that DSA members "have been cultivating connections with Chinese Communist Party officials and agreeing to take pro-China positions."

The magazine based its reporting on records from inside the organization and described what those records contained.

The minutes of the DSA meetings show participants discussing contacts with officials from China's ruling party in the name of "anti-imperialism," with some members saying the organization should avoid topics that are sensitive for Beijing, such as China's threats to invade Taiwan, its security crackdown in Hong Kong and abuses of the Uyghur Muslim minority. They also discuss visits to China. Chinese officials did not take part in the meetings themselves, but met with members in China and encouraged the DSA to set up exchanges, according to the minutes.

One New York-based political activist addressed an October 2025 meeting of the China Working Group of the DSA's International Committee.

"China wants to interface with the DSA," the activist told the meeting. "If we develop a killer two-week itinerary, hire locals and develop further connections with the CPC [Communist Party of China], then we're golden."

The DSA has called for replacing the U.S. Constitution with a new system and for abolishing prisons, the Supreme Court and the police.

Hollywood power broker Ari Emanuel unleashed a profanity-laced tirade against fellow entertainment mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg, accusing the Democrat megadonor of double-crossing him in business and putting his own interests ahead of the Democratic Party.

Appearing on Bill Maher's "Club Random" podcast, Emanuel (who Ari from Entourage was modeled after, plus he's the brother of politician Rahm Emanuel) detailed the decades-old grievances behind his bitter feud with the former Disney executive, including a dispute over basketball tickets and an alleged $1 million proposition involving former President Joe Biden.

Emanuel said the animosity began during Endeavor's early days, when the fledgling talent agency secured coveted Los Angeles Lakers basketball tickets that helped establish its standing in Hollywood.

"You know those basketball tickets that we couldn't afford?" Emanuel recalled, comparing their value to a billboard on Sunset Boulevard.

However, the feud eventually spilled into politics.

Emanuel claimed Katzenberg once offered to secure him a meeting with Biden in exchange for $1 million.

"Do you think I need to give you a million dollars so you can tell Joe Biden that I gave you a million dollars to meet with Joe Biden?" a stunned Emanuel recalled responding, pointing to his family ties to the former president through his brother, Rahm Emanuel, who served as chief of staff to President Barack Obama when Biden was vice president.

Emanuel also criticized Katzenberg's role in Biden's failed 2024 reelection effort, claiming he urged the influential Democrat fundraiser to help push the aging president out of the race.

"You say you got his ear, right? You're the man. You're talking to him all the time," Emanuel recalled telling Katzenberg.

"You got to get him out," Emanuel said he demanded, only to be met with silence.

"He gave us Karen Bass. He gave us this. And now he's just moved on," the superagent continued. "Most of the things he does are not about the situation. It's about Jeffrey and the situation."

"That shit I don't like. I do not like it. And he did try to fuck us over twice. Fuck you," he added.

title: Judge "Highly Likely" To Grant Apple Injunction As OpenAI Fires Back With Its Own Theft Allegations
desc:
Judge "Highly Likely" To Grant Apple Injunction As OpenAI Fires Back With Its Own Theft Allegations

The judge overseeing Apple's trade-secret case against OpenAI said Wednesday he is "highly likely" to grant an injunction barring use of the iPhone maker's proprietary information, a potential setback for the ChatGPT maker's push into consumer hardware, Bloomberg reports.

Ahead of the hearing, however, OpenAI delivered its own accusation: a former employee allegedly took confidential files about an unreleased OpenAI device before returning to Apple, then presented OpenAI's product plans to senior Apple executives. Apple says it found no evidence to substantiate the claims.

The companies that partnered two years ago to bring ChatGPT into Apple's software are now accusing each other of benefiting from the transfer of confidential hardware information. Apparently, the partnership did not include sharing the blueprints.

A Few Bad Apples

Speaking at Wednesday's hearing in San Jose, US District Judge Edward Davila signaled that Apple would likely receive an order preventing use of its proprietary information. But he was less enthusiastic about the company's request for a forensic inspection of all devices and repositories containing Apple trade secrets, describing it as a "huge ask," according to Bloomberg.

Apple attorney John M. Desmarais responded that the company would narrow its inspections to a limited group of former employees now at OpenAI.

"They don't have 400 bad apples, your honor, they have a few bad apples and know who they are," Desmarais said.

The distinction matters: Davila signaled likely preliminary relief, not a final judgment that OpenAI stole Apple's technology. His reported comments also did not amount to an order shutting down OpenAI's hardware program. The practical impact would depend on the terms of an actual injunction.

Apple sued OpenAI, hardware chief Tang Yew Tan and former iPhone engineer Chang Liu in July, alleging a scheme to obtain confidential information covering product design, manufacturing, component technologies, testing methods and its supply chain. Apple says that information is being used to help OpenAI enter the consumer hardware market.

OpenAI denies the allegations and argues that Apple is trying to restrain employees from joining a competitor, portraying "ordinary job interviews" as acts of trade secret misappropriation.

"OpenAI is developing a new family of devices designed for the AI era," the company said in an October court filing quoted by Bloomberg. "OpenAI has no need or desire for Apple's trade secrets."

Its defense also challenges Apple's account of how former employees accessed information. In an earlier public response, OpenAI said current Apple employees had asked Liu to help locate material for their own work. It blamed Apple's account-management practices for leaving former employees with residual access and said Tan had explicitly instructed his team not to use other companies' confidential information.

Those competing explanations are now headed for closer scrutiny. According to Reuters, Davila on Tuesday allowed Apple early access to certain OpenAI digital files and approved expedited depositions of three former Apple employees, including Liu and Tan.

OpenAI Says The Files Were Moving In Both Directions

In its new court filing, OpenAI alleged that an unnamed employee joined from Apple, worked at OpenAI for six months, then returned to Apple after sending more than 100 highly confidential files to personal accounts.

The materials allegedly included images of unreleased hardware, engineering and manufacturing data, supplier information and specifications for cosmetic finishes. Some transfers occurred just after midnight in Singapore on June 2, the employee's final day at OpenAI, the filing said.

OpenAI further alleges that the employee presented its product plans to Apple's senior leadership, including its vice president of operations in Asia. The company says it is concerned that its confidential work could influence Apple's upcoming products.

The filing asks for a case schedule that would allow OpenAI to investigate and, if necessary, pursue counterclaims. It does not itself establish that Apple used the information, nor does it constitute a completed countersuit.

Apple rejected the accusations. The company said it has policies preventing employees from using confidential information belonging to former employers and found no evidence supporting OpenAI's claims, Reuters reported. Apple also accused OpenAI of trying to distract from the evidence underpinning its own lawsuit.

A Hardware Fight With Trillion-Dollar Ambitions

The dispute lands at an awkward time for OpenAI, which is targeting a $1.4 trillion valuation and preparing to go public, according to Bloomberg. Hundreds of Apple employees have moved to OpenAI, turning a software partnership into an increasingly direct contest for hardware talent and expertise.

Bloomberg has reported that OpenAI's first consumer hardware product will be a doughnut-shaped smart speaker priced above $300. People inside the company view it as a distinct, AI-centered device rather than a copy of something Apple plans to release.

But a different-looking product would not, by itself, resolve allegations about the engineering, manufacturing or supplier information used to develop it. Conversely, hiring engineers who know how to build hardware is not the same thing as stealing their former employer's files.

That is the line this case will have to establish. For OpenAI, the immediate risk is an injunction whose scope could complicate its hardware development. For Apple, the new allegations threaten to turn a case about protecting its own secrets into a dispute over how both companies handle everyone else's.

The next generation of AI devices may be revolutionary. The fight over who took what on the way out the door is decidedly old-fashioned.

title: Russia Arrests Japanese Journalist On Espionage Charges, Tokyo Summons Ambassador
desc:
Russia Arrests Japanese Journalist On Espionage Charges, Tokyo Summons Ambassador

Relations between Russian and Japan have been on a downward spiral of late, as Tokyo continues cozying up to the US military as well as NATO, and amid a long-simmering dispute over the Kuril Islands, which Japan identifies as its own Northern Territories.

Russia on Tuesday arrested a Japanese journalist, which the Kremlin says is actually a spy operating on behalf of the Japanese government.

The detained Japanese national has been identified as Yuki Imai, who works for Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper - a regional outlet for Japan's northern island. Hokkaido is one of the country's four main islands and the daily paper he writes for has large dissemination.

The FSB security agency has accused the man of utilizing media sources to gather intelligence, specifically on Russia's defense and intelligence capabilities.

Russian officials say they caught him retaining and storing sensitive data, in a saga that sounds parallel to the saga of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich in 2023-2024.

Imai was reportedly preparing to exit the country upon his detention in the far eastern Sakhalin region.

Tokyo did not immediately issue a full-throated condemnation, only saying that the government is gathering more information on the identity of the detained and the circumstances of the case.

Toward this end, the Russian ambassador to Japan has been summoned, with a protest lodged over the detention, centered on the Kremlin issuing strong accusations yet without providing any explanation to Tokyo.

Japanese and European officials are now seeking access to the detained suspect, even as Russian state media has been airing footage of him in handcuffs.

The footage shows security raiding where he was staying and proceeding to search his electronic devices and belongings while he was held on the floor.

A Japanese journalist has been detained in Russia on suspicion of spying for Japanese intelligence. The arrest comes amid growing tensions between the two countries over the disputed Kuril Islands. https://t.co/0CVKW4aiRb

— Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) October 14, 2026

President Putin had back in August railed against Japan's stance on the Ukraine conflict, which aligns with NATO's perspective.

Putin had said: "Japan, our neighboring country, has used the events in Ukraine as a pretext, without examining the causes of the conflict, to pursue an unprovoked policy against Russia." He had during that time made a highly provocative trip to the disputed Kuril islands. Tokyo strongly protested the visit at the time.

title: Not 'The Onion': Harper's Magazine To Honor NPR CEO Katherine Maher With First Amendment Award
desc:
Not 'The Onion': Harper's Magazine To Honor NPR CEO Katherine Maher With First Amendment Award

Authored by Jonathan Turley via JonathanTurley.org,

Harper's Magazine appears to be competing with The Onion in satire this week. It is awarding its First Amendment prize to NPR CEO Katherine Maher. It is akin to awarding a Second Amendment prize to Gavin Newsom. Maher has long been the very symbol of advocacy journalism and bias. Ironically, she is being given an award after steering NPR into the rocks to keep her job and its ideological bias.

Many of us have written for years about NPR's biased reporting. Not all of this criticism was made out of hostility toward the outlet - many honestly wanted NPR to reverse course and adopt more balanced coverage. That is why, when NPR was searching for a new CEO, I encouraged the board to hire a moderate figure without a history of political advocacy or controversy.

Instead, the board selected Katherine Maher, a former Wikipedia CEO widely criticized for her highly partisan and controversial public statements. She was the personification of advocacy journalism, even declaring that the First Amendment is the "number one challenge" that makes it "tricky" to censor or "modify" content as she would like.

Maher has supported "deplatforming" anyone she deems to be "fascists" and even suggested that she might support "punching Nazis." She also declared that "our reverence for the truth might be a distraction [in] getting things done."

As expected, NPR's bias only got worse. The leadership even changed a longstanding rule barring journalists from joining political protests.

One editor had had enough. Uri Berliner had watched NPR become an echo chamber for the far left with a virtual purging of all conservatives and Republicans from the newsroom. Berliner noted that NPR's Washington headquarters has 87 registered Democrats among its editors and zero Republicans.

Maher and NPR remained dismissive of such complaints. Maher attacked the award-winning Berliner for causing an "affront to the individual journalists who work incredibly hard." She called his criticism "profoundly disrespectful, hurtful, and demeaning."

Berliner resigned, after noting how Maher's "divisive views confirm the very problems at NPR" that he had been pointing out.

Rather than trying to reverse the long slide in its audience, Maher doubled down. She ultimately made the best possible case for defunding NPR. She refused to resign, effectively killing the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Yet, Harper considers her model of media.

In a press release on the awarding of the James C. Goodale First Amendment Award, Harper's declared, "As president and CEO of NPR, Katherine Maher has guided one of America's most important public media institutions through a period of extraordinary political, legal, and financial scrutiny, reaffirming journalism's essential role in a democratic society."

Maher has overseen the continued slide in ratings and revenue. In fairness, NPR's audience has been declining for years. Indeed, that trend has been most pronounced since 2017 - the period when Berliner said the company began to openly pursue a political narrative and agenda to counter Donald Trump. The falling advertising revenue has led to deep staff cuts to deal with budget shortfalls. The shrinking NPR audience remains overwhelmingly white, older, and of course liberal.

title: America Looks Richer Than Ever. What Happens When The Fed's Asset Bubble Bursts?
desc:
America Looks Richer Than Ever. What Happens When The Fed's Asset Bubble Bursts?

Authored by David Stockman via InternationalMan.com,

It is now abundantly obvious that the FOMC and its clumsy rate-pegging and credit printing tools are not remotely fit for purpose.

The real impact is dramatically displayed in the graph below. It shows that after 1987 the growth rate of household assets relative to earned income (i.e. excluding transfer payments) took off like a bat out of hell.

Indeed, as shown in the graph during the heyday of the 1950s through 1987, the nominal value of household assets tracked the growth of earned income almost in lockstep, with the ratio relatively flat through the 37-year period, posting at 5.8X in Q2 1987, up slightly from an average 5.4X ratio during 1950 to 1954, when the US economy moved into its strong post-WWII growth era.

The virtually nonexistent slope of the trend line (solid green below) during that era of unprecedented middle-class prosperity means that had it continued for another 39 years through Q2 2026, the end point ratio today would be just 5.9X, not the actual ratio of 10.0X.

So, yes, the Fed's red-hot printing press did make a whopping difference. To wit, the household and nonprofit sectors today hold the staggering total of $90 trillion more in assets of all types - from owner-occupied residences to cash accounts, bonds and stock portfolios - than would have been the case based on pre-1987 asset-to-income trends.

What this means is that the American household sector did not earn and save its way to the huge gains in assets and net worth reported by the Fed's Flow of Funds data. That is to say, net worth is up from almost $11 trillion to $196 trillion since 1989, but that is not mainly due to savings from the growth of earned income.

As shown, below borrowings helped modestly, rising 5.3% per annum or modestly ahead of the 4.6% per annum growth of personal income ex-transfer payments. But the real catalyst, obviously, was the far faster growth of asset values, which rose at a compound annual rate of 6.1% during the period.

At the end of the day, however, the comparison which says it all is the gap between asset growth at 6.1% per annum and income growth of just 4.6%. In a word, assets grew 35% faster than income over that three and one-half decade period because, well, the Fed inflated them with its red-hot printing presses.

For want of doubt, we show the opposite trend in the household savings data, meaning that the American public has not saved its way to riches since Alan Greenspan discovered the printing presses in the basement of the Eccles Building soon after he took office in the midst of Black Monday's 23% collapse of the Stock Market on October 19, 1987.

The juxtaposition of the savings graph below and asset graph above, in fact, tells you all you need to know. Since 1975, the true household savings rate - measured as personal savings divided by household income less transfer payments (used as the denominator here because the government's 160 million Welfare State beneficiaries save virtually nothing on a net basis) has been plodding steadily lower (dotted red line), from an average of 13.3% of income in 1975 to 6.7% of income at present.

At the same time, the constant dollar level of savings pencils out anemically, indeed. The growth rate (blue lines) in real terms has been just 0.6% per annum since 1975.

So, no, America did not save its way to $196 trillion of net worth after the era of Keynesian monetary central planning commenced in October 1987. The Fed inflated asset prices to a fare-the-well.

Of course, all this inflated net worth is just the half of it. The more onerous dimension lies in who got it or in the distribution. In that regard, the graph below speaks for itself. Since Q1 1989, household net worth has risen by an aggregate of $154 trillion.

As it happened, however, the bottom 50% got 3% of the gain, while the top 1% harvested 32% of the loot. Some earnest commentators are now mystified as to why the hoary doctrine of socialism seems to be making a comeback in certain quarters of American politics.

The geniuses at the Fed, however, should not be confused at all. It's all their handiwork.

In the land of the central bank printing presses, the rich do get richer, indeed, and not because they earned it on an honest free market operating based on sound money.

In fact, the chart above reflects the true failure of Greenspanian central banking. And when the massive inflationary bubbles embodied in this graph above finally do blow sky-high, don't blame it on the free market.

In short, what amounts to free money has been the real culprit all along.

title: Useless Without Transmission: DOE Backs $581 Million TVA Grid Expansion
desc:
Useless Without Transmission: DOE Backs $581 Million TVA Grid Expansion

On the same day we asked how much of the grid’s bill is really AI’s, the Department of Energy offered a partial answer.

@TVAnews and @ENERGY are supporting readily-available, affordable energy that powers Tennessee and the nation. @POTUS is lowering costs for over 2 million families and businesses while bringing new innovation and employment to the Volunteer State to the tune of 800 jobs.

— Senator Bill Hagerty (@SenatorHagerty) October 13, 2026

On Tuesday, DOE said it plans to help the Tennessee Valley Authority fund 84 transmission and distribution projects across eight states to add about 2.5 gigawatts of grid capacity. The award totals roughly $581 million, with $250 million in federal money and $331 million from TVA.

“America’s electric grid cannot become a roadblock to economic growth,” said Katie Jereza, who heads DOE’s Office of Electricity.

Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly went further, blaming “years of misguided energy policies under the previous administration” for leaving the bulk power system “less robust than it should be.”

From $250 Million To $10.5 Billion

The announcement for TVA support from the DOE is alongside the ongoing SPARK program under the GRIP program… If the acronyms are starting to blur together, here is the simple version:

  • Tuesday’s award is for $250 million, written to TVA and its local power companies.
  • SPARK, DOE’s acronym for “Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades,” is the bigger, nationwide program. It puts $1.9 billion of federal money, plus $3.35 billion in cost share, into 31 projects in 26 states that will reconductor or rebuild more than 1,500 miles of existing lines and free up over 23 GW of capacity. TVA’s slice is about $80 million to upgrade roughly 125 miles of lines in Tennessee, Alabama and North Carolina with advanced conductors, adding about 1,900 MW.
  • GRIP, the Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships program, is the even bigger $10.5 billion pot created by the 2021 infrastructure law, and it pays for both SPARK and the new award announced Tuesday afternoon.

Add TVA’s two awards together and it has nearly $741 million in planned grid investment for more than 4,300 MW of added grid capacity.

The Real Bottleneck

As we just covered, the hyperscalers are fighting over how much of the grid’s bill is theirs, with one telling Senate staff that shared upgrades provide a “system benefit which should be shared among all ratepayers.”

Tuesday’s award is that argument in practice, with taxpayers and utility customers splitting the cost of wires everyone uses, on a national grid where, by the senators’ own count, about a third of transmission and half of distribution infrastructure is “near or beyond its useful life.”

You can build all the combined-cycle gas plants, reactors and geothermal wells you want, and line up every data center and electrified factory in the country to buy their output. If the grid can’t carry the power from one to the other, none of it matters.

"there is currently a 3.7-year wait in the US just to get permission to connect to the power grid. Before a single cable is laid or transformer is purchased, AI data centers are stuck in a massive traffic jam." - Goldman it's ok, hyperscalers can just recycle electricity, same way they do revenue

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) August 28, 2026

PJM has already blatantly exposed where the real problem is, as they cried desperately about a need for emergency power. When Constellation showed up with the Three Mile Island reactor restart, PJM told the once-connected nuclear plant to wait patiently for a few years while they set up the connection.

TVA is about to learn that lesson, at scale. Its new long-term plan suggests the region will need 11 to 32 GW of additional generation by 2040. TVA already has 4,120 MW of new capacity under construction, floated as much as 26 GW of new gas in its June draft, and was picked last December for a $400 million DOE award to deploy a newly-licensed GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 small modular reactor at Clinch River.

Every one of those megawatts still needs a way to actually get transported from supply to demand. No amount of new generation fixes a lack of transmission.

Goldman: Power Is “The Primary Risk”

Goldman has been making the same point all year, and it has singled out Tennessee. In May, the commodities team flagged Tennessee as one of the markets “likely to see constrained data center additions since the market is already critically tight.”

In February, the same team told clients that local opposition to data centers was not the real threat: “Ultimately, we believe power tightness remains the primary risk that could slow the US in the AI race with China.” And Goldman now sees behind-the-meter generation powering a quarter of all data centers by 2030.

In other words, a quarter of the industry may simply stop waiting for the grid.

title: Dowd: "Investment Bubbles Are A Feature Of Capitalism, Not A Bug"
desc:
Dowd: "Investment Bubbles Are A Feature Of Capitalism, Not A Bug"

Authored by Ed Dowd via Ed Dowd's Beyond The Narrative Substack,

On Friday October 9th Bloomberg published an article titled "Jeffries' Chris Wood Sees 'Massive Capital Destruction' in AI." His view is that the most likely long-term outcome of the AI boom is massive capital destruction in the US, with market share shifting to cheaper open-source Chinese models. Wood has mostly got it right in my opinion except for two differences. My first difference is that Chinese models are not the only open-source models available and that western open-source models are closing the gap. Secondly, while his view correctly flags the overbuild and the competitive pressure from lower-cost alternatives what it leaves out is the long history of innovative technology infrastructure bubbles and the reliable pattern that follows them which is:

excitement/mania → overinvestment → financial collapse → distressed assets → recapitalized cheap infrastructure fuels the next economic wave.

In regard to the AI bubble, I believe we are currently in the overinvestment phase with cracks emerging. Let us look at some historical examples to illustrate the pattern and see if we can glean what the future of this current bubble might look like.

The US Railroad Bubble

In the decades after the Civil War, railroads became the transformative technology of the era. Capital, much of it European, flooded in. Between the late 1860s and early 1870s, tens of thousands of miles of track were laid, often into sparsely settled or unprofitable territory. Speculative financing, land grants, and the expectation of endless growth created a classic mania. Early projects showed strong returns, which attracted more money into later, riskier lines built far ahead of demand. When financing dried up, highlighted by the failure of Jay Cooke's bank in marketing Northern Pacific bonds, the Panic of 1873 followed. More than 100 railroads went bankrupt in the ensuing years, banks failed, and investors were wiped out. The depression lasted years. Yet the physical tracks remained. The surviving and reorganized network became the backbone of American industrial expansion, enabling efficient movement of goods, people, and capital that powered decades of growth. The overbuilt infrastructure, once distressed and recapitalized, proved far more valuable to the broader economy than the paper losses suggested.

The 1920s Utility Bubble

The 1920s electrification boom followed a similar script. Central-station utilities expanded rapidly, and holding companies consolidated regional systems into large, leveraged empires. Electricity generation and revenues grew dramatically as the technology moved from novelty to infrastructure. Utility stocks soared and became a major part of the market. Holding companies facilitated access to capital and technical expertise, but the structures were opaque, and capacity was built aggressively. The 1929 crash and subsequent Depression exposed the leverage and accounting. Samuel Insull's empire collapsed in spectacular fashion, and the Dow Jones Utilities Average plunged. Reforms including the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 broke up the largest structures and shifted the industry toward regulated regional monopolies. What remained was a vastly expanded electrical grid and generation capacity. Widespread electrification transformed industry, homes, and productivity for the rest of the century. The bust was painful for equity and debt holders; the long-term economic payoff from cheap, abundant power was enormous.

The Dotcom Bubble

The most recent and directly analogous example is the late 1990s telecom fiber buildout during the Dotcom era. Carriers and infrastructure firms poured hundreds of billions into fiber-optic networks, switches, and related equipment, largely financed with debt and encouraged by forecasts of internet traffic doubling every few months. Capacity vastly exceeded near-term demand. After the bubble burst, market values collapsed, many telecoms went bankrupt, and bandwidth prices fell sharply. A large portion of the newly laid fiber sat "dark" or unlit. Through bankruptcies and recapitalizations, that physical infrastructure was acquired at deep discounts, often pennies on the dollar. The resulting cheap broadband made business models viable that would have been prohibitively expensive otherwise. Google, YouTube, Facebook, Apple's smartphone ecosystem, Netflix, software-as-a-service, and cloud services all scaled on that excess capacity. Without the overbuilding and subsequent distress, Web 2.0 as we know it does not happen at the same speed or cost. The capital destruction was real but the residual infrastructure seeded the next wave of growth.

AI Bubble (Yes it is a bubble!)

I believe we are now in the AI infrastructure equivalent of the overinvestment phase. Massive capital is flowing into data centers, chips, power, and related equipment. The sheer scale of spending is turning advanced AI models into a commodity faster than many equity and debt investors appear to appreciate. Chinese open-source models are already applying downward pricing pressure, consistent with the Jefferies view. Cracks are visible. In my Substack piece "Wall Street's AI Capex Party...It's 2 AM & The Bar Is About to Close!", the signals included stalled private credit funding for the buildout, cracking enterprise demand as promised productivity gains fail to materialize at scale, looming power constraints that are becoming the binding limit rather than chip supply, and open-source pricing pressure that compresses margins.

Additional recent indicators from public commentary reinforce this: circular deals in which AI companies run negative free cash flow and rely on debt investors to keep purchasing chips at elevated prices; recent analyses showing major players cannot cover contracted compute commitments under realistic revenue assumptions; and narrative shifts such as space based data centers that paper over terrestrial grid and power bottlenecks. Growth rates implied by current valuations look vulnerable once the second derivative of funding and utilization slows. It is not a question of not if the bubble bursts but when it bursts.

Credit Markets Always End Infrastructure Buildouts

Debt and credit have been central to every one of these infrastructure buildouts. In the railroad boom, bonds financed the majority of the expansion, often more than three-quarters of the capital. When those markets stopped absorbing new bond issues (e.g. Jay Cooke & Co. could no longer place Northern Pacific bonds) the credit system seized up. Then bank runs followed, the New York Stock Exchange closed for ten days, and within two years roughly a third of outstanding railroad bonds had stopped paying interest. The equity markets lagged in this period...credit markets ended the railroad party abruptly.

The 1920s utility expansion followed the same pattern on a different scale. Samuel Insull's holding company pyramid relied on layers of debt and bank loans secured by the securities of the operating companies themselves (financial engineering). Once revenues softened and the banks refused to roll the notes in 1932, the structure collapsed into receivership. In this period the equity markets led the credit markets first with the 1929 crash then credit followed later.

In the telecom fiber boom, carriers raised hundreds of billions in bonds and used vendor financing and circular deals to keep the buildout going. Credit markets ultimately marked the end of the buildout but equities peaked in March of 2000 before credit. Credit spreads later widened sharply in 2001 and 2002, defaults clustered in the sector for years, and bondholders recovered roughly twenty cents on the dollar in many cases. When lenders stopped funding incremental capacity, the overinvestment phase ended and the financial collapse began.

The same dynamic is now visible in the AI buildout, where private credit has stalled, circular debt structures are proliferating, off balance sheet financing is growing and early signs of stress are appearing in CCC junk credit markets. Whether equity markets lead or lag this cycle remains to be seen but the case could be made that given the tremendous amount of passive equity investing the discounting mechanism of equity could lag and credit leads this time.

Bottom Line

Innovative technology capex cycles repeat themselves because human nature has not changed. Mania and excitement give way to overinvestment, which produces financial collapse and distressed assets. Those assets then become the cheap foundation for the next economic wave. Those who believe in cycles and a constant human nature may want to protect themselves accordingly and reduce exposure in the AI complex where risk-reward no longer makes sense. Then when the bust does arrive watch for the opportunities that emerge from the ashes where durable longer-term value will be created.

Bubbles are a feature of capitalism, not a bug. They destroy capital in the short run and, through the process of overbuilding and recapitalization, often leave behind the physical and technical foundation for longer-term productivity gains. The pattern is consistent throughout history...though the timing and severity may vary. The long-term outcome for the economy is usually more favorable than the peak-to-trough equity charts imply and a net positive over time.

"What has been will be again, what has been done will be done again; there is nothing new under the sun." Ecclesiastes 1:9

title: Bank Of America Tumbles After Trading Miss Across The Board
desc:
